title: THE GYPSY COUNCIL and OTHERS v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
summary: In the case of The Gypsy Council and Others v. the United Kingdom, the applicants included two organisations—the Gypsy Council for Education, Culture, Welfare and Civil Rights and Friends, Families and Travellers—alongside Mr. Thomas O’Doherty and Mr. Terence Green, both members of the Romany Gypsy community. The case centred on the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller groups whose traditional cultural gatherings, such as the Horsmonden Horse Fair in Kent, faced prohibition by local authorities, threatening their cultural expression and community life. The Horsmonden Horse Fair, a significant annual event for the Romany Gypsy community, had been held for at least fifty years, with claims of a tradition spanning three centuries. In 2000, following concerns about public order and disruption, the local Parish Council sought and obtained a prohibition order under the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994, effectively banning the fair within a five-mile radius. The applicants challenged this order in the High Court, arguing it disproportionately interfered with their rights under Articles 6, 11, and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The European Court of Human Rights found that while the prohibition order interfered with the right to freedom of assembly, the measure was lawful, pursued legitimate aims, and was proportionate, given the disruption anticipated. The Court declared the application inadmissible, finding no violation of the Convention. This case highlights the ongoing tension between the protection of Roma and Traveller cultural traditions and public order concerns, reflecting broader historical challenges faced by these communities in asserting their rights across Europe.
